verdict.rationale: Three independent grammatical engines converge on the proposition. John 10:35 predicates incapacity of failure directly of the written text: 'Scripture is not able to be broken' (ou dunatai luthenai he graphe), where 'is able' (dunamai) stands in the present indicative (an ongoing, simple statement of fact, not a wish) negated by 'not' (ou), and 'to be broken' (luo) is an aorist passive infinitive (a completed-action verbal noun in the passive voice), so the clause reads 'the Scripture is-not-able to-be-broken', with 'the writing' (graphe, the writing itself) as grammatical subject. Isaiah 55:11 uses a negated efficacy construction, 'it shall not return empty' (lo yashuv reyqam), the word from God's mouth shall not return empty-handed, where 'empty' (reyqam) is the standard term for a null, result-less outcome (Genesis 31:42, Exodus 23:15, Ruth 1:21), and the 'but rather' (ki im) pivot asserts it shall instead 'accomplish' (asah) what God 'delights in' (hafets). Matthew 5:18 and Luke 16:17 add the durability sayings: the emphatic double negation 'by no means' (ou me) with aorist subjunctive (a completed-action mood expressing strong denial of future possibility) 'pass away' (parelthe) and the comparative 'easier' (eukopoteron) place the survival of the smallest text-token, 'iota' (the smallest Greek letter, a hapax meaning a word occurring only once in the entire Bible) and 'serif stroke' (keraia, occurring only twice), above the survival of heaven and earth. The vocabulary asserts that divine speech and the inscripturated text cannot fail of their purpose; what the words do not delimit is the precise scope of that reliability, which is where readers diverge.

scripture.force: The single most precise infallibility statement in the canon. The clause 'Scripture is not able to be broken' (ou dunatai luthenai he graphe) predicates the incapacity of failure directly of the written text. MorphGNT (the critical edition of New Testament morphological tagging) parses 'is able' (dunatai) as present middle/passive indicative third singular (an ongoing, simple statement of fact in the form 'it is') of 'be able' (dunamai), a plain statement of fact, 'is not able'. It parses 'to be broken' (luthenai) as aorist passive infinitive (a completed-action verbal noun in the passive voice) of 'loose, annul, break' (luo, to be loosed, annulled, broken), with the negation 'not' (ou). The grammatical subject is 'the writing' (he graphe, the writing, the Scripture), nominative (the subject form), so the sentence asserts the Scripture cannot be broken. The same verb 'loose' (luo) is used in Matthew 5:19 for breaking a commandment, an intra-canonical lexical bridge linking this denial to the durability sayings. The one lexical caveat is that 'loose' (luo) is polysemous (carries multiple meanings) across its 44 canon occurrences (untie a colt, release a prisoner, dissolve the temple, destroy the works of the devil), but the subject 'writing' (graphe) and the contrast clause 'the word of God came' (ho logos tou theou egeneto, the word of God came) disambiguate it cleanly to the sense annul or nullify.

Negated efficacy construction (a grammatical form denying that an action can fail to produce its result). The 'word' (dabar) issuing from God's mouth shall 'not return' (lo yashuv) 'empty-handed' (reyqam) but rather shall 'accomplish' (asah) what God 'delights in' (hafets) and shall succeed in the matter for which he sent it. The lexeme 'empty' (reyqam) occurs 15 times in the canon and consistently means without result, empty-handed, in vain (Genesis 31:42, Exodus 23:15, Ruth 1:21, 2 Samuel 1:22), so its negation by 'not' (lo) is a categorical denial that divine speech can fail of its purpose. The 'but rather' (ki im) clause is the strong adversative pivot ruling out null-result. ETCBC-BHSA (a syntactic database of the Hebrew Bible) parses the clause with the negation function (Nega) and a purpose complement (Cmpl) explicitly marked. This grounds infallibility on the efficacy axis (the word cannot fail to do its work) rather than on the truthfulness axis (the word is true), which is the property the proposition targets.

Solemn amen-formula plus a comparative durability claim. MorphGNT (the critical edition of New Testament morphological tagging) parses 'pass away' (parelthe) as aorist active subjunctive third singular (a completed-action mood expressing strong denial of future possibility) of 'pass away' (parerchomai, pass away), and the central verb cluster is negated by the emphatic double negation 'by no means' (ou me), the strongest available Greek denial of future possibility, governed by 'until' (heos an, until). The lexemes 'iota' (iota, a hapax meaning a word occurring only once in the entire Bible, the smallest letter) and 'serif stroke' (keraia, occurring only twice, the serif stroke distinguishing similar letters) are deliberately at the granular extreme of text-token vocabulary, asserting indissolubility at the level of orthographic detail (the smallest written marks). The form is a comparative that places the survival of the least visible feature of the law above the survival of heaven and earth. The terminal clause 'until all comes to pass' (heos an panta genetai, until all comes to pass) is the one element the grammar leaves open and is read in more than one way.

Independent Synoptic version of the same saying. MorphGNT (the critical edition of New Testament morphological tagging) parses 'easier' (eukopoteron) as a comparative adjective (easier) and frames a relative-difficulty argument: it is easier for heaven and earth 'to pass away' (parelthein, aorist active infinitive, a completed-action verbal noun) than for one 'serif stroke' (keraia) of the law 'to fall' (pesein, aorist active infinitive of 'fall' (pipto)). Luke substitutes 'fall' (pipto, to fall, perish) for the gospel parallel's 'come to pass' (ginetai), reinforcing the non-failure side of the same claim with a different but synonymous lexeme. The shared vocabulary core ('law' (nomos), 'serif stroke' (keraia), 'heaven' (ouranos), 'earth' (ge), 'pass away' (parerchomai)) gives multi-Synoptic convergence on the textual-durability proposition without verbal dependence that would collapse it to a single witness.

Cross-reference verified in the lexical store (TSK CrossRef and OpenBible with 232 votes, the densest cross-reference edge in this set). Jesus' direct claim: 'heaven and earth shall pass away, but my words shall by no means pass away' (ho ouranos kai he ge pareleusontai, hoi de logoi mou ou me parelthosin). MorphGNT (the critical edition of New Testament morphological tagging) parses 'shall pass away' (pareleusontai) as future middle indicative (a future-tense statement of fact) and 'should pass away' (parelthosin) as aorist active subjunctive plural (a completed-action mood expressing strong denial of future possibility, in the plural) under the emphatic 'by no means' (ou me). Lexically parallel to Isaiah 55:11's 'it shall not return empty' (lo yashuv reyqam): the negated passing-away of divine speech, here applied to Jesus' own 'words' (logoi) rather than the inscripturated 'law' (nomos).

Cross-reference verified in the store (TSK CrossRef and OpenBible, 10 votes). Synoptic parallel to Matthew 24:35 with the identical lexical core: heaven and earth shall pass away, but my words shall by no means pass away ('shall by no means pass away', ou me parelthosin, the emphatic double negation with aorist active subjunctive plural). Multi-Synoptic attestation of the cosmos-versus-word durability formula on the same emphatic double negation.

Cross-reference verified in the store (TSK CrossRef and OpenBible, 7 votes). Contrasts the withering of grass and fading of flower (created realities) with 'the word of our God' (devar eloheinu) which 'shall stand' (yaqum, qal which is the simple active form of the Hebrew verb, of 'stand, endure' (qum), to stand, endure) 'forever' (le-olam). The verb 'stand' (qum, 575 canon occurrences) is the positive lexical counterpart to the negated 'it shall not return empty' (lo yashuv reyqam) of Isaiah 55:11: divine speech stands where created order fades, the same a fortiori (an argument from greater to lesser) the gospel sayings make.

Cross-reference verified in the store (TSK CrossRef and OpenBible, 22 votes). 'Forever, O LORD, your word stands fixed in the heavens' (Le-olam YHWH devarekha nitsav ba-shamayim). The niphal which is the Hebrew passive form participle 'stands fixed' (nitsav, from 'be set, stationed, firm' (natsav, set, stationed, firm, 67 canon occurrences)) lexically asserts the established, non-mutable status of YHWH's word, with 'in the heavens' (ba-shamayim) tying word-stability to the most permanent created locus. Writings-genre attestation alongside prophecy and gospel gives pan-canonical (spread across the whole Bible) reach.

Cross-reference verified in the store (TSK CrossRef and OpenBible, 23 votes). 'The one who establishes the word of his servant' (Meqim devar avdo) and 'the counsel of his messengers he completes' (atsat malakhav yashlim). The hiphil which is the Hebrew causative form (to cause to do) 'establishes' (meqim, cause to stand, from 'stand' (qum)) is the positive lexical parallel to the negated 'it shall not return empty' (lo yashuv reyqam) two chapters later, the same Isaian theology of efficacious divine speech.

Cross-reference verified in the store (TSK CrossRef and OpenBible, 26 votes). The Noahic-oath comparison: 'as I swore' (nishbati, from 'swear' (shava)) that the waters of Noah should no more cover the earth, so have I sworn that I will not be angry. The chapter's appeal to the inviolability of divine oath supplies the framework for 55:11's claim that the divine word cannot fail.

complicating_texts.resolution: The terminal clause 'until all things come to pass' (heos an panta genetai, until all things come to pass) is grammatically open and is read in two main lexical-syntactic directions: a temporal-limit reading (the Torah's force runs until an eschatological accomplishment, after which something changes) and a perpetuity reading (the law endures as long as heaven and earth endure). The text-durability claim about 'iota' (the smallest Greek letter) and 'serif stroke' (keraia) is independent of which is taken. Under either reading the statement denies that the smallest feature of the text can fail or be annulled prior to its full accomplishment, which is exactly the infallibility property in view. So the open clause affects the temporal scope of Torah-application, not the non-failure assertion.

The verse speaks of 'the word' (dabar) going out from God's mouth, not directly of written Scripture as a fixed canonical artifact, and lexically 'word' (dabar, 1368 occurrences) covers oracle, command, and divine self-communication broadly. The infallibility claim derives from the pattern that whatever counts as divine speech does not return empty. The transfer to the written text is closed lexically by John 10:35, where the non-broken predicate is applied to 'the writing' (he graphe, the writing itself), and by Matthew 5:18 and Luke 16:17, which apply the non-passing-away predicate to the inscripturated 'law' (nomos). So the spoken-versus-written gap is bridged by the very anchor set, not assumed.

The verb 'loose' (luo) in 'is not able to be broken' (ou dunatai luthenai) is polysemous (carries multiple meanings) across its 44 canon occurrences (untie, release, dissolve, destroy, break a commandment). In isolation the clause could in principle carry a softer sense than annul. Context disambiguates: 'the writing' (he graphe) is the subject, the parallel clause 'the word of God came' (ho logos tou theou egeneto) frames Scripture as God's own coming word, and Matthew 5:19 uses the same verb 'loose' (luo) for breaking a commandment, fixing the sense here as nullify or annul. The polysemy is the one genuine lexical soft spot but it is resolved by subject and co-text, so it does not reach verdict-level doubt; it bears on how readers describe the scope of the reliability, not on whether reliability is asserted.

variants.note: The lexical store holds 116 VariantUnit nodes, all confined to 3 John (the ingested ECM (the critical edition of New Testament textual variants) window). None of the four anchor verses (John 10:35, Isaiah 55:11, Matthew 5:18, Luke 16:17) nor the cross-referenced durability texts (Matthew 24:35, Luke 21:33, Isaiah 40:8, Psalm 119:89, Isaiah 44:26, Isaiah 54:9) fall in that window, so not_in_ecm_scope is honestly true. The key lexemes ('writing' (graphe), 'loose' (luo), 'be able' (dunamai), 'pass away' (parerchomai), 'iota' (the smallest Greek letter), 'serif stroke' (keraia), 'empty' (reyqam)) are textually stable across the major manuscript tradition with no verdict-altering variation; no variant signal was invented.

competing_lens_verdicts.framework: plenary-infallibility (reliability extends to every assertion of the text)
competing_lens_verdicts.rationale: Reads John 10:35 'is not able to be broken, the Scripture' (ou dunatai luthenai he graphe) as an unqualified predicate of the whole written 'writing' (graphe), and Matthew 5:18 'iota' (the smallest Greek letter) and 'serif stroke' (keraia) as marking indissolubility down to the smallest orthographic unit (the smallest written marks). On this lens the words assert non-failure with no built-in limit, so the property holds of whatever the text asserts.

competing_lens_verdicts.framework: purpose-or-faith-and-practice scope (reliability is anchored to the text's saving and covenantal intent)
competing_lens_verdicts.rationale: Reads Isaiah 55:11 as the controlling grammar: the word shall not return 'empty' (reyqam), that is, it shall not fail to accomplish the purpose ('delights in', hafets, what God delights) for which it was sent. On this lens the non-failure predicate is intrinsically purpose-indexed (it cannot fail at what it is for) rather than a claim about every incidental detail. This lens still affirms the proposition as stated, since the proposition itself names matters of faith and practice.

competing_lens_verdicts.framework: redemptive-historical reading of Matt 5:18 heos an panta genetai
competing_lens_verdicts.rationale: Reads the open terminal clause 'until all comes to pass' (heos an panta genetai) as a temporal hinge: the Torah's binding form endures until it is fully accomplished in Christ, after which its mode of application shifts. This lens does not deny that the text cannot fail prior to and within that accomplishment; it locates the durability claim inside redemptive history rather than as a flat timeless perpetuity. The non-failure of the word is affirmed; the lens differs only on the temporal frame of its application.

hermeneutics.notes: Verdict rests on grammatico-historical reading (interpretation by grammar and historical setting) of three constructions: the present-indicative (ongoing, simple statement of fact) incapacity statement 'is not able to be broken' (ou dunatai luthenai) in John 10:35, the negated-efficacy clause 'it shall not return empty' (lo yashuv reyqam) in Isaiah, and the emphatic 'by no means' (ou me) plus aorist subjunctive (a completed-action mood expressing strong denial of future possibility) and comparative 'easier' (eukopoteron) in the Synoptic durability sayings. Analogia scripturae (Scripture interpreting Scripture) operates through OT-NT lexical bridging ('word' Hebrew (dabar) and Greek (logos), the parallel non-passing-away formula, the shared verb 'loose' (luo) across John 10:35 and Matthew 5:19). Progressive revelation (truth unfolding stage by stage across the canon) appears in the move from spoken oracle (Isaiah 55) to written Torah and 'writing' (graphe) (Matthew 5, Luke 16, John 10). The three competing lenses all affirm the proposition as stated; they differ on the scope and temporal frame of the reliability, not on whether the text asserts it.

stem_audit.notes: The stem is descriptive of a property (cannot fail to accomplish what God intends, incapable of misleading in matters of faith and practice) rather than prescriptive of authority. It does not smuggle sola scriptura (the principle of Scripture as sole authority), canonical scope, mode of inspiration, or inerrancy in scientific or historical detail. The qualifier in matters of faith and practice is a standard lexical-functional scope statement, not a denominational signal, and it matches the purpose-indexed grammar of Isaiah 55:11 (the word does not fail of its intent). VERDICT-CHANGED: no, verdict unchanged from the prior file: affirms remains true. The enrichment adds John 10:35 as the lexically sharpest anchor ('is not able to be broken, the Scripture' (ou dunatai luthenai he graphe), the written Scripture cannot be broken), distinguishes the infallibility or non-failure axis ('loose' (luo), 'pass away' (parerchomai), 'it shall not return empty' (lo yashuv reyqam)) from the truthfulness and inerrancy-scope axes, corrects the cross-reference vote counts against the queried store (the prior file labeled all edges votes=1, but OpenBible attests them at 7 to 232 votes), and states the competing scope lenses symmetrically where the prior file left that list empty.

lay_summary: This proposition asks whether Scripture cannot fail to accomplish what God intends and cannot mislead in matters of faith and practice. The clearest single statement is John 10:35, where Jesus says the Scripture cannot be broken. In Greek this is 'Scripture is not able to be broken' (ou dunatai luthenai he graphe). The verb 'be able' (dunamai) sits in the plain present tense (is not able), negated by 'not' (ou), and the verb 'loose' (luo, to loosen, annul, break) is a passive infinitive, with the writing itself (graphe) as the subject. So the sentence flatly denies that the text can be annulled. The same verb 'loose' (luo) is used elsewhere for breaking a commandment, which ties this denial to the rest of the pattern. Isaiah 55:11 supplies the matching idea from the other side: the word that goes out from God's mouth shall not return empty, where the word for empty 'empty-handed' (reyqam) means without result, the same word used when someone is sent away empty-handed. It cannot fail to do its work. Then Matthew 5:18 and Luke 16:17 add the durability sayings, using the smallest possible text-tokens ('iota' (iota), the smallest letter, which occurs only once in the canon, and 'serif stroke' (keraia), the tiny serif stroke, occurring only twice) and the strongest Greek negation 'by no means' (ou me) to say the least visible mark of the law will outlast heaven and earth. Cross-references verified in the data reinforce this across the canon: the word of our God stands forever, your word is fixed in the heavens, and heaven and earth will pass but my words will not. The pattern is dense, spans prophecy, writings, and the Gospels, and the verses are textually stable, so the affirmative is high-confidence. Where readers diverge is not whether the text claims it cannot fail, but how far that reach extends. One reading takes it of every assertion; another anchors it to the purpose for which the word was sent (matters of faith and practice), which is what the Isaiah grammar emphasizes; and the open phrase until all is accomplished in Matthew leaves room for debate about the time frame, not about the non-failure itself.
